4423.prule: One culminative word stress, never final, always on the first or second syllable. Disyllables: stress on the first syllable regardless of lexical tone or vowel length. Words of three or more syllables: stress on the second syllable by default (phonologically toneless words, e.g. [iˈpuːrɛi] 'dress', [naˈqasɨrɛi] 'scorpion', [iːˈbɨxi] 'breathes', [taːˈtasəi] 'splits'), but on the first syllable when that syllable carries the lexical H tone ([ˈúːʎiɟɨ] 'his maternal grandmother'). Position is thus set by word size plus lexical tone, not by weight (JIPA 2021, the author's later refereed description). The earlier AMP 9 conference paper (same author, same speakers, PDF dated March 2021) formulated the same surface facts as 'stress on the first heavy syllable (long vowel, consonant or glide coda), otherwise on the second', NON-FINALITY >> IAMBIC-RHYTHM >> STRESS-TO-WEIGHT, with heavy-initial second-stressed words treated as lexical-L exceptions (*ALIGN(HEAD/LOW)); JIPA drops weight and treats those words as regular toneless/second-H cases.

4423.tone: JIPA 2021: 'a tonal language with a single phonological tone: the high tone H' (privative /H/), 'low tonal density' (not all morphemes specified), H culminative (at most once per phonological word), H 'only occurs in the first two syllables of a root and in some suffixes'; 'a high pitch is also a correlate of stress in toneless words, but stress and high pitch could not coincide when lexical H is present' (in H-final disyllables stress stays initial, identified by vowel quality, intensity and native-speaker judgment). AMP 9 2021 analyses the same pitch facts as a privative /L/ on the long first vowel of L.H disyllables, with stress cued by an intonational H* that docks on the stressed syllable unless a lexical L blocks it (constraint *ALIGN(HEAD/LOW)); 1200-entry lexical base, F0 on 265 H.L and 427 L.H disyllabic tokens. Both analyses agree on the surface: a single non-final word stress in the first or second syllable, initial in disyllables, and in longer words on the first syllable only when it carries the pitch prominence (JIPA: lexical H; AMP: weight, minus L-toned exceptions). Bascom 1982: 272 (SIL grammar sketch, in the copy consulted) had claimed 'Stress is noncontrastive. It is freely fluctuation in many words.' with two tones (high marked, low unmarked); Bascom 1959 'Tonomechanics' (paywalled) is the equipollent H/L source; Kim 1997 (WCCFL 15, not located) derived tone from metrical stress.

4423.cfw: Gil Burgoin's first-hand acoustic description of the Baborigame dialect (2021, JIPA Illustration and AMP 9 paper) establishes Northern Tepehuan as a tone language with a single culminative high tone and predictable, non-contrastive stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the first or second syllable of longer words, and the only dissent is Bascom's one- remark that stress 'fluctuates freely in many words', an older impressionistic note that Gil Burgoin 2021 reports is not borne out by the word lists in Bascom & Molina 1998. 4424.prule: Stress falls on the first or the second syllable of the word, i.e. within the root (never posterior to it): the inherited Pomoan second-syllable (root) stress survives in some disyllabic roots and in prefix+root stems (šiʔˈba 'body', fu-ʔdú 'float'), but has shifted to the first syllable in many other disyllabic roots (ˈbehše 'deer', dúwe 'night'); Buckley states that the conditioning of the shift is undetermined, and his 2014 slides list the same forms transcribed with either placement 'cited without a difference in context' (šúʔu-ka: ~ šuʔú-ka: 'coyote', málaʔ ~ maláʔ 'ashes'), possible rightward shift under suffixation (má:ti 'day' / ma:tí-min 'sunrise'), possible sentence-rhythm effects, and conclude 'but at present, pattern remains uncertain'. No dominant pattern is asserted.

4426.heavy: Syllables containing long vowels (written as geminates) are heavy = branching nucleus; 'aw, ay, uy and iy represent diphthongs, which behave like the long vowels (ie. branching nuclei) for the purposes of stress assignment'; 'All other syllables, with few exceptions -to be discussed- are light' (p.195). 4426.dflt: penultimate main stress (word-level); in all-light trisyllables penult with an optional initial variant; disyllables initial = penult
4426.prule: Word-level main stress on the penultimate syllable by default, with quantity sensitivity: in words of four or more syllables a word-final long vowel or diphthong following a light penult 'usually' (formalised as optionally) takes main stress, but the penult always wins when the last two syllables are both heavy; disyllables are always initial(=penult)-stressed regardless of weight; in trisyllables a heavy penult (long vowel or closed syllable) is always main-stressed, a light penult after a heavy initial never is (initial stress), a heavy final after two light syllables optionally takes main stress, and all-light trisyllables vary between penultimate and initial stress.
4426.srule: Secondary stress on the word-initial syllable; weaker (tertiary) stresses on alternating syllables preceding the penult, footed right-to-left in binary quantity-sensitive left-dominant feet (all-light words: 1010, 10010, 101010, 1001010 with main stress on the penult); every long vowel or diphthong not bearing main stress also carries secondary stress ('length consistently attracts secondary stress').

tn.quote: En el mixteco del norte de Tlaxiaco, algunas palabras se pronuncian casi iguales; solamente el nivel de la voz hace la diferencia. El nivel, que se llama “tono”, puede ser alto (agudo), bajo (grave) o medio. Generalmente, no habrá confusión entre palabras que difieren solamente en el tono porque la oración o contexto en que se usan ayuda a distinguirlas. tn.translation: In Northern Tlaxiaco Mixtec some words are pronounced almost the same; only the level of the voice makes the difference. The level, called 'tone', can be high (acute), low (grave) or mid. Generally there is no confusion between words that differ only in tone because the sentence or context in which they are used helps distinguish them. Despite the distinction tone can make between two or more words, in this variety of Mixtec no special symbol is being used to mark tone. ndee 'cost' / ndee 'go out' / ndee 'go down' / ndee 'until' ...

4436.dloc: Section 2.4 'Stress', p. 413 (the whole section sits on this page, 2.5 Phonotactics opens p. 414); scope statement section 2.1 p. 407; language inventory section 1.4 p. 403 (language (f)); west-coast consonant-final remark section 2.5 p. 414.
4436.prule: No rule fixed. Working from 19th-century recorders' accent diacritics (Walker, Norman), Milligan's orthographic remark, Tindale's transcriptions, the Fanny Cochrane Smith cylinders and Crowley's 1972 recordings, the authors infer, hedged ('it appears'), that disyllables are stressed on the first syllable and trisyllables on the first or the second syllable with no conditioning given; their 'only general conclusion' is negative: any syllable except the last can bear stress. Stated for 'Tasmanian' collectively; p. 407 says the phonology 'is based mainly on the mid-eastern and south-eastern languages... It seems likely that most of our remarks will also apply to languages in other parts of Tasmania'. None of the six evidence sources is specifically north-western (Milligan's vocabularies include some two hundred words 'assigned to north-west and western tribes', which Crowley and Dixon say correspond poorly with earlier vocabularies from those areas, p. 397); nothing stress-specific is said about language (f).

4444.dq: Stress is marked after the syllable; the main stress is marked with " e.g. do"ki; secondary stress is marked witn ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable). (The examples are isolated words and the 'Tone and Stress of the Past Tense' section lists verb forms by syllable count, but the source never states a domain or contrasts word with phrase prominence.)

4444.prule: No positional stress rule. In Abraham's 1929 Hausa-modelled, pre-phonemic analysis 'stress' is a notational derivative of the tone melody: §29 (p. 114) equates stressed syllables with High tone and unstressed with Low, and in his own transcriptions (p. 205, read) the main-stress mark (") always sits after a syllable bearing the highest tone level present in the word (High if any, otherwise Mid: go"woyi' High, Low, Mid; indu"wo Low, Mid, Low; fullu"woyi' Low, Mid, Low, Mid; laduruŋ"go Low, Low, Mid, Low; sikitu"woyi' Low, Low, Mid, Low, Mid), though not necessarily after the first such syllable (mo"tu'wo and du"ru'wo High, High, Low, but wo'du"woyi' High, High, Low, Mid), and the secondary mark (') after the other non-Low syllables, whether High (mo"tu'wo) or Mid (go"woyi'). Placement therefore follows the lexical/grammatical tone melody, not syllable count or weight. Modern descriptions (Gimba 1998, 2000; Gimba, Ali, Bah & Schuh 2009; Schuh 2005) treat Bole as a two-tone (H/L) register language with downdrift, tone spreading and Low Tone Raising, and never mention stress.
4444.srule: Abraham 1929 names and marks a 'secondary stress' (') but gives no placement rule ('secondary stress is marked witn ' e.g. tam"baya' (last syllable)', p. 204); in his transcriptions the mark follows the non-Low syllables other than the main-stressed one (go"woyi' H-L-M, mo"tu'wo H-H-L, p. 205; Past-tense pronoun suffixes 'all have stress except -ni which has Low Tone', p. 214), i.e. it is a tone correlate. Superseded: Schuh, Gimba & Ritchart 2010 (pp. 226, 235) find no lexical or phrasal stress in Bole, hence no secondary stress.

4447.prule: Mixed 'tono acentual' system ('stress to high tone', Wetzels & Meira). Lexical tone contrast on monosyllabic lexemes: L (default, unmarked) vs HL vs LH; a polysyllabic morpheme carries at most one H (contour split left-to-right over the first two syllables). Intensity stress is predictable and non-contrastive: in bi- and trisyllabic monomorphemic words it falls on the syllable bearing H; when the word has no H it falls on the first syllable from the left. Since H sits on the first syllable in most such words (H.L, H.L.L; L.L and L.L.L stressed initially), stress is in effect word-initial and demarcates the prosodic word; the author says this 'could be interpreted as a fixed, non-contrastive stress' (p.233).

tn.quote: Las características prosódicas de la lengua Nɨkak corresponden a un sistema mixto, que combina el contraste tonal lexical en monosílabos, y la marcación del acento de intensidad. ... en Nɨkak se presentan secuencias segmentales idénticas o análogas monosilábicas, en los cuales se realizan tres tipos de tonos, que son tono bajo sin notación (L), descendente ̂ (HL) y tono ascendente ̌ (LH). tn.translation: The prosodic characteristics of Nɨkak correspond to a mixed system, which combines lexical tonal contrast in monosyllables with the marking of intensity stress. ... in Nɨkak there are identical or analogous monosyllabic segmental sequences on which three types of tone are realised, namely low tone, unmarked (L), falling ̂ (HL) and rising tone ̌ (LH). Low tone is realised by default, but within monosyllabic morphemes it contrasts with the HL and LH tones. ... In polysyllabic words the tones split from left to right
